CATSIB DIF Detection Procedure

Source: R/catsib.R, R/print.R
catsib.Rd

This function performs DIF analysis on items using the CATSIB procedure (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004), a modified version of SIBTEST (Shealy & Stout, 1993). The CATSIB procedure is suitable for computerized adaptive testing (CAT) environments. In CATSIB, examinees are matched on IRT-based ability estimates that have been adjusted using a regression correction method (Shealy & Stout, 1993) to reduce statistical bias in the CATSIB statistic caused by impact.

Usage

catsib(
  x = NULL,
  data,
  score = NULL,
  se = NULL,
  group,
  focal.name,
  item.skip = NULL,
  D = 1,
  n.bin = c(80, 10),
  min.binsize = 3,
  max.del = 0.075,
  weight.group = c("comb", "foc", "ref"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  missing = NA,
  purify = FALSE,
  max.iter = 10,
  min.resp = NULL,
  method = "ML",
  range = c(-5, 5),
  norm.prior = c(0, 1),
  nquad = 41,
  weights = NULL,
  ncore = 1,
  verbose = TRUE,
  rho.screen = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'catsib'
print(x, digits = max(2L, getOption("digits") - 5L), ...)

Arguments

x

A data frame containing item metadata (e.g., item parameters, number of categories, IRT model types, etc.). See est_irt() or simdat() for more details about the item metadata. This data frame can be easily created using the shape_df() function. x is needed to estimate the abilities internally, that is, when score = NULL or purify = TRUE. It can be NULL when score and se are supplied and purify = FALSE; the items are then labeled item.1, item.2, and so on. Default is NULL.

data

A matrix of examinees' scored responses (0 or 1). Rows represent examinees and columns represent items, in the order of the rows of x when x is supplied.

score

A numeric vector of examinees' ability estimates (theta values), in the same row order as data, with their standard errors in se. The estimates should be based on the item parameters in x. If NULL, abilities and standard errors are estimated internally with est_score() using method, range, norm.prior, nquad, weights, and ncore, and x must be supplied. When purify = TRUE, abilities and standard errors are re-estimated internally at every purification iteration, so a supplied score is used only in the initial analysis. A missing value in score excludes the examinee from the analysis, also during purification, with a warning. Default is NULL.

se

A numeric vector of the standard errors of the ability estimates in score, in the same order. The standard errors are used to estimate the reliability of the ability estimates in the regression correction (see Details). It must be supplied when score is supplied, and it is ignored when score = NULL. Default is NULL.

group

A numeric or character vector indicating examinees' group membership. The length of the vector must match the number of rows in the response data matrix.

focal.name

A single numeric or character value specifying the focal group. For instance, given group = c(0, 1, 0, 1, 1) and '1' indicating the focal group, set focal.name = 1.

item.skip

A numeric vector of item positions (columns of data, or rows of x), or a logical vector with one value per item, identifying the items to exclude from the analysis. Skipped items still contribute to the ability estimates, but their results (beta, se, z.beta, p, and the contingency table) are set to NA, and they are never flagged or removed during purification; their sample sizes (n.ref, n.foc, and n.total) are still reported, as in rdif() and crdif(). If NULL, all items are analyzed. Default is NULL.

D

A scaling factor in IRT models, used only when abilities are estimated internally. Default is 1.

n.bin

A numeric vector of two positive integers giving the maximum and minimum numbers of equal-width bins (intervals) of the corrected ability scale, in this order (the maximum must not be smaller than the minimum). For each item, the number of bins starts at the maximum and decreases by one until the condition set by max.del is met; if it is not met with the minimum number, the minimum number is used. Default is c(80, 10). See Details.

min.binsize

An integer of 2 or more specifying the minimum number of examinees of each group in a bin. A bin is used in the computation of \(\hat{\beta}\) only if it contains at least min.binsize examinees of both the reference and focal groups who responded to the item. Default is 3, the value used by Nandakumar and Roussos (2004). See Details.

max.del

A numeric value specifying the maximum proportion of the examinees of each group who responded to the item that may be excluded because they fall in bins that are not used (see min.binsize). The number of bins is reduced until the excluded proportion is at most max.del in both groups. It must be at least 0 and less than 1. Default is 0.075. See Details.

weight.group

A character string specifying the target ability distribution used to weight the bins in \(\hat{\beta}\) and its standard error: "comb" for the combined distribution of the reference and focal groups, "foc" for the focal group, or "ref" for the reference group. The weight of a bin is the proportion of the examinees of the target distribution in the bins used who fall in that bin. Default is "comb".

alpha

A numeric value specifying the significance level (\(\alpha\)) of the two-sided test of the CATSIB statistic. An item is flagged when its p-value is less than or equal to alpha. The comparison uses unrounded p-values, although the p-values reported in dif_stat are rounded to four decimal places. Default is 0.05.

missing

A value indicating missing responses in the data set. Default is NA.

purify

Logical. Indicates whether to apply a purification procedure. Default is FALSE.

max.iter

A positive integer specifying the maximum number of iterations allowed for the purification process. Default is 10. Each iteration removes one item, so max.iter should be at least as large as the number of items expected to be flagged. If the limit is reached while flagged items remain, a warning is issued, the complete element of the purification results is FALSE, and the items flagged in the last iteration are added to the flagged items. This argument is not passed to est_score().

min.resp

A single nonnegative number, usually a positive integer, specifying the minimum number of item responses that an examinee must have to be used in the analysis. All responses of examinees with fewer than min.resp (but at least one) responses are set to NA before the ability estimation, in the initial analysis and at every purification iteration, also when score is supplied, and these examinees are excluded from the analysis. A warning reports the number of examinees excluded in the initial analysis, and one warning at the end of the purification reports the examinees excluded during it. A large min.resp can leave a group with fewer than two ability estimates within range in a later purification iteration, which stops the purification with a warning. If NULL, no minimum is applied. Default is NULL. See Details for more information.

method

A character string indicating the scoring method used to estimate the abilities when score = NULL and in every purification iteration. Available options are:

  • "ML": Maximum likelihood estimation

  • "MLF": Maximum likelihood estimation with fences

  • "WL": Weighted likelihood estimation (Warm, 1989)

  • "MAP": Maximum a posteriori estimation (Hambleton et al., 1991)

  • "EAP": Expected a posteriori estimation (Bock & Mislevy, 1982)

The methods "EAP.SUM" and "INV.TCC" of est_score() are not supported, because they do not give an ability estimate for each response pattern. "ML" or "WL" is recommended, because the regression correction assumes unbiased ability estimates (see Details). Default is "ML".

range

A numeric vector of length two specifying the lower and upper bounds of the ability scale. It is used when abilities are estimated internally with the scoring methods "ML", "MLF", "WL", and "MAP". In addition, ability estimates at or beyond these bounds are excluded when the mean, the variance, and the error variance of the ability estimates are computed for the regression correction (see Details); this also applies when score is supplied, so range should match the bounds used to obtain score. Default is c(-5, 5).

norm.prior

A numeric vector of length two specifying the mean and standard deviation of the normal prior distribution. These values are used to generate the Gaussian quadrature points and weights. Ignored if method is "ML" or "WL". Default is c(0, 1).

nquad

An integer indicating the number of Gaussian quadrature points to be generated from the normal prior distribution. Used only when method is "EAP". Ignored for "ML", "WL", and "MAP". Default is 41.

weights

A two-column matrix or data frame containing the quadrature points (in the first column) and their corresponding weights (in the second column) for the latent variable prior distribution. The weights and points can be conveniently generated using the function gen.weight().

If NULL and method = "EAP", default quadrature values are generated based on the norm.prior and nquad arguments. Ignored if method is "ML", "WL", or "MAP".

ncore

An integer specifying the number of logical CPU cores used by est_score() when abilities are estimated internally. The test statistics themselves are not computed in parallel. Default is 1.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, the progress of the purification procedure is printed to the console. Default is TRUE.

rho.screen

Logical. If TRUE, the ability estimates whose squared standard error is equal to or greater than the variance of the ability estimates of their group are left out of the computation of the mean, the variance, and the error variance that define \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\) in the regression correction. These examinees are still matched and used to compute \(\hat{\beta}\). If FALSE, \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\) is computed from all ability estimates within range, as in Nandakumar and Roussos (2004, Equation 7). The screening is not part of the original procedure and is added in irtQ. Default is TRUE. See Details.

...

Additional arguments passed to est_score() when abilities are estimated internally, for example tol. The est_score() arguments se, max.iter, and missing cannot be passed this way, because catsib() uses arguments with these names for its own purposes.

digits

Not used; kept for consistency with the other print methods.

Value

This function returns an object of class "catsib", which is a list with the following five components:

no_purify

A list containing the results of the DIF analysis without applying a purification procedure. This list includes:

dif_stat

A data frame with one row per item and the columns id, beta, se, z.beta, p, n.ref, n.foc, and n.total: the item ID, the CATSIB statistic \(\hat{\beta}\), its standard error, the standardized statistic, the two-sided p-value, and the numbers of examinees of the reference and focal groups in the bins used to compute \(\hat{\beta}\), and their sum. A positive \(\hat{\beta}\) indicates DIF in favor of the reference group. All values are rounded to four decimal places.

dif_item

A numeric vector of the positions (columns of data) of the flagged items, or NULL if no item is flagged.

contingency

A list with one element per item, named by item ID. Each element is a data frame with one row per bin used to compute \(\hat{\beta}\) and the columns bin (the interval of corrected ability estimates), n.ref, prop.ref, var.ref, n.foc, prop.foc, and var.foc (the number of examinees, the proportion of correct responses, and the sample variance of the item responses of each group in the bin), n.total, weight (the weight of the bin), beta (the weighted difference in the proportions of correct responses), and var.beta (the contribution of the bin to the squared standard error), followed by a row whose bin is Total, with the totals of n.ref, n.foc, n.total, beta, and var.beta. The element is NA for a skipped item.

purify

A logical value indicating whether purification was requested (the purify argument).

with_purify

A list with the results of the purification procedure. All elements are NULL when purify = FALSE. The elements are:

dif_stat

A data frame with the same columns as no_purify$dif_stat and an additional column n.iter. For an item removed during purification, the row reports the statistics from the iteration in which the item was removed, and n.iter is that iteration minus 1 (0 for an item removed on the basis of the initial analysis). For the other items, the row reports the statistics from the last iteration, and n.iter is the number of that iteration. If no item is flagged in the initial analysis, this is no_purify$dif_stat with n.iter = 0.

dif_item

A numeric vector of the positions (rows of x) of the items flagged by the CATSIB statistic, sorted in ascending order. It contains the items removed during purification and, if the purification stops before it is complete (see complete) with items left, the items flagged in the last iteration (iteration n.iter). It contains all items if every item is flagged. NULL if no item is flagged in the initial analysis.

n.iter

The number of purification iterations performed (0 if no item is flagged in the initial analysis). An iteration after which the statistics cannot be recomputed (see Details) is not counted.

complete

A logical value. TRUE if the procedure stopped because no remaining item was flagged (including the case in which no item is flagged in the initial analysis), and FALSE if it stopped because max.iter was reached, because every item was flagged, because a group had fewer than two ability estimates within range, or because no remaining item had a usable bin.

contingency

A list with the same structure as no_purify$contingency. For an item removed during purification, it holds the table from the iteration in which the item was removed; for the other items, it holds the table from the last iteration. If no item is flagged in the initial analysis, this is no_purify$contingency.

alpha

A numeric value indicating the significance level (\(\alpha\)) used for the tests.

call

The matched function call.

Details

CATSIB (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004) estimates the amount of DIF in an item as \(\hat{\beta} = \sum_{k} (\hat{P}_{R,k} - \hat{P}_{F,k}) \hat{p}_k\), where \(\hat{P}_{R,k}\) and \(\hat{P}_{F,k}\) are the proportions of correct responses of the reference and focal groups in bin k of the corrected ability scale, and \(\hat{p}_k\) is the weight of bin k (see weight.group). A positive \(\hat{\beta}\) indicates DIF in favor of the reference group. The standard error of \(\hat{\beta}\) is estimated from the sample variances of the item responses in each bin and group (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004, Equation 10), and the test statistic \(\hat{\beta} / \mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta})\) (z.beta) is compared with the standard normal distribution in a two-sided test. Examinees are matched on \(\hat{\theta}^{\ast}\), an estimate of the expected value of \(\theta\) given \(\hat{\theta}\) obtained by the regression correction described below. The range of \(\hat{\theta}^{\ast}\) is divided into K equal-width bins, and examinees are classified into the bins by their \(\hat{\theta}^{\ast}\). A bin is used only if it contains at least min.binsize examinees of both groups who responded to the item; Nandakumar and Roussos (2004) required at least three, which is the default.

To choose the number of bins K, catsib() follows the rule of Nandakumar and Roussos (2004). For each item, K starts at a large value (80 by default), and if more than 7.5% of the examinees of either group who responded to the item would be excluded because they fall in bins that are not used, K is reduced by one, until at most 7.5% of each group is excluded. Nandakumar and Roussos (2004) did not allow fewer than 20 bins, but they reported that a minimum of 10 bins reduced the estimation bias caused by excluding examinees from sparse bins. catsib() therefore uses a minimum of 10 bins by default; if the condition is not met with the minimum number, the minimum number is used. The maximum and minimum numbers of bins are set by n.bin, and the maximum proportion of excluded examinees by max.del.

Li and Stout (1996) and Nandakumar and Roussos (2004) used the combined distribution of the two groups as the target ability distribution, which is the default of weight.group. See Nandakumar and Roussos (2004) for further details about the CATSIB method.

Because the ability distributions of the reference and focal groups can differ (impact), matching examinees directly on \(\hat{\theta}\) would bias \(\hat{\beta}\) toward DIF in favor of the group with the higher mean ability. CATSIB therefore applies a regression correction separately in each group G (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004, Equation 7): \(\hat{\theta}^{\ast} = \bar{\hat{\theta}}_G + \hat{\rho}^2_G (\hat{\theta} - \bar{\hat{\theta}}_G)\), where \(\bar{\hat{\theta}}_G\) is the mean of the ability estimates in group G and \(\hat{\rho}^2_G = 1 - \hat{\sigma}^2_{e,G} / \hat{\sigma}^2_{\hat{\theta},G}\) is the estimated reliability of the ability estimates in group G. Here \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{e,G}\) is the mean of the squared standard errors (se) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{\hat{\theta},G}\) is the variance of the ability estimates in group G. Ability estimates at or beyond a bound of range are excluded when these quantities are computed, because their standard errors are not meaningful; this also applies when score is supplied, so range should match the bounds used to obtain score.

Because \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{e,G}\) is a mean of squared standard errors, a few examinees with very large standard errors, typically examinees with very low or very high scores whose abilities are poorly determined, can make \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\) much smaller than the reliability of the other ability estimates, or even negative. The corrected ability estimates then shrink too much toward the group mean, which distorts the matching and can inflate the Type I error rate, particularly during purification. When rho.screen = TRUE (the default), the examinees whose squared standard error is greater than or equal to \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{\hat{\theta},G}\) of their group are left out of the computation of the mean, the variance, and the error variance that define \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\), unless fewer than two estimates would be left. For these examinees the individual reliability \(1 - SE^2 / \hat{\sigma}^2_{\hat{\theta},G}\) is zero or negative, that is, their ability estimates carry no information about their abilities beyond the spread of the group. They still receive corrected ability estimates and are used in the matching and in the computation of \(\hat{\beta}\). This screening is not part of the original procedure (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004) and is added in irtQ; set rho.screen = FALSE to compute \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\) from all ability estimates within range as in the original procedure. Even with the screening, the Type I error rate of CATSIB can be higher than the nominal level, and in data without DIF the purification can increase the number of false positives. In addition, \(\hat{\rho}^2_G\) is bounded to the interval \([0.05, 1]\), and a warning is issued when its unbounded value is below 0.05. A negative value would reverse the order of the ability estimates within a group, and a value near zero would place almost all corrected ability estimates of a group in one bin. This bound is not part of the original procedure and is added in irtQ. Even with the bound, the corrected ability estimates of the two groups may not overlap when the groups differ in ability; then no bin contains enough examinees of both groups for an item, \(\hat{\beta}\), its standard error, z.beta, and the p-value are NA, one warning names the items, and the items are not flagged.

The regression correction assumes that the ability estimates are unbiased, that is, that \(\hat{\theta}\) equals \(\theta\) plus an error with mean zero. The Bayesian estimates ("MAP" and "EAP") are already shrunk toward the prior mean, so the correction shrinks them a second time. Use "ML" or "WL", especially when the abilities are re-estimated during the purification.

CATSIB, like SIBTEST (Shealy & Stout, 1993), was designed and evaluated for uniform DIF (Nandakumar & Roussos, 2004). Because \(\hat{\beta}\) sums signed differences across bins, differences of opposite sign can cancel, so its sensitivity to nonuniform or mixed DIF is limited, and results for items suspected of nonuniform DIF should be interpreted with caution.

Nandakumar and Roussos (2004) did not propose a purification procedure for CATSIB, but catsib() can apply an iterative purification procedure in the manner of Lim et al. (2022). It requires x. When purify = TRUE, at each iteration the flagged item with the smallest p-value is removed (the p-values are compared on the log scale), the abilities and their standard errors are re-estimated from the remaining items with the scoring method specified in method, and the CATSIB statistics of the remaining items are recomputed. Supplied score and se are therefore used only in the initial analysis. The procedure stops when no remaining item is flagged or when max.iter iterations have been performed. If no item is flagged in the initial analysis, no iteration is performed. If every item is flagged, the procedure stops with a warning, because no item is left to estimate the abilities, and complete is FALSE. The procedure also stops with a warning and complete = FALSE when, after an item is removed, a group has fewer than two ability estimates within range, which the regression correction requires, or no bin contains enough examinees of both groups for any remaining item; the remaining items then keep the results of the previous iteration, and the items flagged in that iteration are added to the flagged items.

Scoring based on a small number of item responses can lead to large standard errors, potentially reducing the accuracy of DIF detection with CATSIB. The min.resp argument excludes such examinees. For example, if min.resp = 5, examinees who responded to fewer than five items (but at least one) have all their responses treated as missing (i.e., NA) before the abilities are estimated, in the initial analysis and at every purification iteration, and a warning reports their number in the initial analysis. As a result, their ability estimates are missing, and they are not used in the computation of the CATSIB statistics. When score is supplied, the scores of these examinees are also treated as missing. During purification, the count is based on the items that remain after the flagged items are removed, and an examinee excluded once stays excluded. If min.resp = NULL, a score is computed for any examinee with at least one valid item response.

Examinees whose ability estimate is NA, such as examinees without any item response or examinees with NA in a supplied score, are excluded from the analysis, and a warning reports the number of examinees with item responses who are excluded because of a missing value in score; these examinees stay excluded during purification. During purification, an examinee whose remaining responses are all removed with the flagged items, or who has fewer than min.resp responses to the remaining items, has no ability estimate and is excluded, and one warning at the end reports the number of such examinees. The sample sizes n.ref and n.foc count only the examinees in the bins used to compute \(\hat{\beta}\).

The group argument should contain exactly two distinct values, one for the reference group and one for the focal group identified by focal.name, and its length must equal the number of rows in data. Examinees with NA in group are excluded from the analysis. The function stops when the reference group or the focal group has fewer than two ability estimates within range, because the regression correction cannot be computed.

The print method of this class has an argument digits that is not used; the statistics are printed rounded to three decimal places.

Methods (by generic)

  • print(catsib): Print method for an object of class catsib (given as x). It prints the flagged items and the CATSIB statistics of the analyses without and with purification, rounded to three decimal places.

References

Bock, R. D., & Mislevy, R. J. (1982). Adaptive EAP estimation of ability in a microcomputer environment. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 431-444. doi:10.1177/014662168200600405 .

Hambleton, R. K., Swaminathan, H., & Rogers, H. J. (1991). Fundamentals of item response theory. Newbury Park, CA: Sage.

Li, H.-H., & Stout, W. (1996). A new procedure for detection of crossing DIF. Psychometrika, 61(4), 647-677. doi:10.1007/BF02294041 .

Lim, H., Choe, E. M., & Han, K. T. (2022). A residual-based differential item functioning detection framework in item response theory. Journal of Educational Measurement, 59(1), 80-104. doi:10.1111/jedm.12313 .

Nandakumar, R., & Roussos, L. (2004). Evaluation of the CATSIB DIF procedure in a pretest setting. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 29(2), 177-199. doi:10.3102/10769986029002177 .

Shealy, R., & Stout, W. (1993). A model-based standardization approach that separates true bias/DIF from group ability differences and detects test bias/DTF as well as item bias/DIF. Psychometrika, 58(2), 159-194. doi:10.1007/BF02294572 .

Warm, T. A. (1989). Weighted likelihood estimation of ability in item response theory. Psychometrika, 54(3), 427-450. doi:10.1007/BF02294627 .

Examples

# \donttest{
# Load required package
library("dplyr")
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘dplyr’
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

## Uniform DIF Detection
###############################################
# (1) Simulate data with true uniform DIF
###############################################

# Import the "-prm.txt" output file from flexMIRT
flex_sam <- system.file("extdata", "flexmirt_sample-prm.txt", package = "irtQ")

# Select 36 3PLM items that are non-DIF
par_nstd <-
  bring.flexmirt(file = flex_sam, "par")$Group1$full_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(.data$model == "3PLM") %>%
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::row_number() %in% 1:36) %>%
  dplyr::select(1:6)
par_nstd$id <- paste0("nondif", 1:36)

# Generate four new items to contain uniform DIF
difpar_ref <-
  shape_df(
    par.drm = list(a = c(0.8, 1.5, 0.8, 1.5), b = c(0.0, 0.0, -0.5, -0.5), g = rep(0.15, 4)),
    item.id = paste0("dif", 1:4), cats = 2, model = "3PLM"
  )

# Introduce uniform DIF in the focal group by shifting b-parameters
difpar_foc <-
  difpar_ref %>%
  dplyr::mutate_at(.vars = "par.2", .funs = function(x) x + rep(0.7, 4))

# Combine the 4 DIF and 36 non-DIF items for both reference and focal groups
# Therefore, the first four items now exhibit uniform DIF
par_ref <- rbind(difpar_ref, par_nstd)
par_foc <- rbind(difpar_foc, par_nstd)

# Generate true theta values
set.seed(123)
theta_ref <- rnorm(500, 0.0, 1.0)
theta_foc <- rnorm(500, 0.0, 1.0)

# Simulate response data
resp_ref <- simdat(par_ref, theta = theta_ref, D = 1)
resp_foc <- simdat(par_foc, theta = theta_foc, D = 1)
data <- rbind(resp_ref, resp_foc)

###############################################
# (2) Estimate item and ability parameters
#     using the aggregated data
###############################################

# Estimate item parameters
est_mod <- est_irt(data = data, D = 1, model = "3PLM")
#> Parsing input... 
#> Estimating item parameters... 
#>

#> Computing item parameter var-covariance matrix... 
#> Estimation is finished in 1.9 seconds. 
est_par <- est_mod$par.est

# Estimate ability parameters using ML
theta_est <- est_score(x = est_par, data = data, method = "ML")
score <- theta_est$est.theta
se <- theta_est$se.theta

###############################################
# (3) Conduct DIF analysis
###############################################
# Create a vector of group membership indicators
# where '1' indicates the focal group
group <- c(rep(0, 500), rep(1, 500))

# (1) Compute the CATSIB statistic using provided scores and standard errors,
#     without purification (x can be NULL in this case)
dif_1 <- catsib(
  x = NULL, data = data, D = 1, score = score, se = se, group = group, focal.name = 1,
  weight.group = "comb", alpha = 0.05, missing = NA, purify = FALSE
)
print(dif_1)
